Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Opinion Taxing the Unborn: Why Ghana’s best enterprise reforms must reach the tax counter Source : Emmanuel Tetteh 9 November 2026 2:17pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
On 4 November 2026, the @Office of the Registrar of Companies (ORC) published two notices that barely registered above the daily political noise. Exercising its powers under Section 289(5) of the Companies Act, 2019 (Act 992), the Registrar dissolved 323 companies in Companies Bulletin Volume 49. Another 453 entities were placed on a three-month countdown in Volume 48. They joined thousands of silent businesses struck off the corporate roll over the past four years.
Public commentary usually treats this corporate graveyard as a morality play about Ghanaian entrepreneurship. We are told that founders register companies on a whim, print complimentary cards, and abandon their statutory filings out of sheer indiscipline.
Follow the paper trail from Ridge to the tax office, and a very different story emerges.
Walk three kilometres from the ORC’s headquarters to a Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) Taxpayer Service Centre. Watch what happens when two young software engineers incorporate a company in January, spend six months building a product on personal savings, and apply for a Tax Clearance Certificate (TCC) in July so they can bid for their first commercial contract.
They have issued zero invoices. Their corporate bank account holds little more than the minimum opening deposit. Under the Income Tax Act, 2015 (Act 896), corporate income tax is levied on chargeable income, which means net profit. A company with zero revenue has zero profit. It legally owes zero corporate tax.
Yet those founders often walk out of the branch office carrying a signed clearance letter and an unbudgeted tax bill.
Why? Because to unlock the TCC required by the Public Procurement Act, 2003 (Act 663) or a corporate vendor portal, the startup collides with Section 14 of the Revenue Administration Act, 2016 (Act 915). That clause bars the Commissioner-General from issuing clearance unless satisfied that all taxes due are paid, or that the applicant has made "arrangements satisfactory to the Commissioner-General."
Worse still, the automated digital link between the ORC and the GRA activates a company’s tax profile the moment its Certificate of Incorporation is printed. The revenue system treats incorporation as the immediate start of taxable trade.
If the founders did not know they had to log onto the portal every month to file Nil PAYE returns, Nil withholding schedules, and a Q1 Nil Provisional Assessment the week they registered, Section 73 of Act 915 has already been ticking. The penalty is 500 currency points (GH¢500) per unfiled return, plus GH¢10 for every day the default continues.
Tax officials will rightly point out that Section 122(3) and (5) of Act 896 allows any company to file a Nil provisional estimate with a statement of reasons. On paper, that is true.
In practice, two operational traps close the door. First, Section 71 of Act 915 penalises any taxpayer whose provisional estimate falls below 90 per cent of their eventual actual chargeable income. That makes a zero estimate risky for a startup hoping to land a contract in the fourth quarter. Second, desk officers routinely invoke their "best judgement" powers under Section 122( of Act 896, backed by the discretionary gatekeeping of Section 14 of Act 915, to question a Nil estimate when a TCC is requested for a commercial tender.
With a bid deadline 48 hours away, a desperate founder has no leverage. They pay an arbitrary GH¢3,000 or GH¢5,000 "provisional deposit on account" just to get the certificate and submit their bid.
When you price compliance higher than evasion, you are not collecting revenue; you are subsidising informality.
What makes this operational habit so costly is that it actively undermines some of the smartest legislative upgrades Ghana has enacted in years.
Across government, policymakers have worked hard to modernise the business climate. On 15 July 2026, the President assented to the Ghana Investment Promotion Authority Act, 2026 (Act 1173). The new law replaces the old GIPC Act, transforms the Centre into a full Authority, and bravely abolishes crippling minimum foreign capital requirements for joint ventures and wholly foreign-owned service and tech companies.
In the same progressive spirit, the Ghana Startup and Innovation Bill has been crafted to give early-stage ventures breathing room through structured incentives and patient capital. On 1 September 2026, the Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 2026 (Act 1178) took effect, raising the Modified Taxation Scheme threshold to GH¢750,000 so small sole proprietors can pay a simple 3 per cent presumptive turnover tax. Even within the GRA, the pilot rollout of the Integrated Tax Administration System (ITAS) in April 2026 is a laudable effort to retire fragmented software and give taxpayers a single self-service dashboard.
The policy intent at the top is clear: lower the barriers to entry and help formal businesses grow.
Down in the engine room of the tax code, however, the collection machinery still runs on an older instinct: collect the cash upfront on gross transactions, and sort out whether the business actually owed the money months later.
Trace the cash-flow statement of a young Ghanaian service company that survives its first year.
First, before earning its first cedi, it parts with scarce seed money as a provisional deposit just to get a bidding TCC.
Second, under the Value Added Tax Act, 2025 (Act 1151), while goods retailers enjoy a GH¢750,000 registration threshold, service providers, including software firms, engineers, and consultants, must register for VAT from day one regardless of turnover.
Third, once the startup wins a contract above GH¢2,000 and delivers, the client acts as a statutory withholding agent under Section 116(2) of Act 896. The client deducts 7.5 per cent on services, 5 per cent on works, or 3 per cent on goods from the gross invoice value before paying the startup. If the client is a designated VAT withholding agent under Section 56 of Act 1151, another 7 per cent Withholding VAT is held back at source.
After paying cloud hosting bills, developer salaries, office rent, and power, its actual net profit margin before tax is 8 per cent. At a 25 per cent corporate income tax rate (plus the 2.5 per cent Growth and Sustainability Levy on profit before tax), its true income tax bill for the year is 2.2 per cent of gross turnover (0.275 × 8% = 2.2%).
Yet the state has already taken 7.5 per cent of its gross turnover at source.
The state has over-collected by 5.3 per cent of the company's total revenue.
Multiply that across thousands of low-margin SMEs, local contractors, and zero-rated exporters under Act 1151, and you see why the GRA General Refund Account exists. The system collects excess cash upfront and promises to refund the difference later.
Except "later" is getting harder to reach. In April 2025, the Revenue Administration (Amendment) Act, 2025 (Act 1129) reduced the statutory cap on the GRA General Refund Account from 6 per cent to 4 per cent of total tax revenue.
In the first seven months of 2026, actual refund payouts dropped to just 1.7 per cent of gross tax revenue. Because Section 69(3) of Act 915 sweeps any unspent balance in the Refund Account back into the Consolidated Fund at year-end, delayed refunds quietly pad government cash flow at the expense of private working capital.
Borrowing at zero per cent interest from the cash flow of young private enterprises is not an entirely frictionless path to national job creation.
Seen through this lens, the hundreds of dormant companies struck off by the ORC on 4 November 2026 are not a mystery. They are a predictable engineering outcome.
Consider what happens when those two software engineers lose the tender they paid a provisional TCC deposit to chase in Year 1:
The GH¢3,000 provisional deposit they paid to secure their bidding TCC sits frozen on their tax profile as an overpayment credit. Demanding a cash refund under Section 68 of Act 915 triggers a mandatory audit that no one-year-old startup wants to host.
While the founders pause operations for a year to rebuild their product, the ORC-GRA compliance clock keeps running. Every month they forget to log in and file Nil returns, Section 73 penalties pile up at the GRA. Meanwhile, filing an annual return at the ORC under Section 126 of Act 992 requires attaching audited financial statements signed by an external auditor, an expensive requirement for a bank account with zero revenue.
By Year 2, when the founders finally land a paying client, they discover their dormant company has accumulated GH¢15,000 in combined GRA and ORC administrative penalties on zero turnover.
At that moment, the founder faces a perverse choice. Paying GH¢15,000 to rescue a company that has never traded makes no commercial sense when incorporating a brand-new company at the ORC costs less than GH¢1,000. So they walk away from the first company, leave it to die on the ORC roll, and register a new one.
What most founders do not realise is that Section 289(6) of the Companies Act, 2019 (Act 992) carries a hidden sting: even after the ORC dissolves a struck-off company, the personal liability of every director and officer remains alive and enforceable.
Our compliance workflow unintentionally pushes honest entrepreneurs to treat companies like disposable SIM cards, while leaving legal landmines under their names.
We have a real opportunity to fix this. The government has already shown bold reformist energy with the GIPA Act, 2026 (Act 1173), the ITAS digital rollout, and the upcoming Ghana Startup and Innovation Bill.
To ensure those flagship laws succeed in the real economy, and to reverse Ghana’s recent six-place slip to 87th in the 2026 Global Startup Ecosystem Index, we must align day-to-day tax administration with our investment ambitions.
Look at what happened to the Young Entrepreneurs tax exemption under the Sixth Schedule of Act 896 (as amended by Act 956). That well-intentioned law gave founders under age 35 a five-year corporate tax holiday in ICT, manufacturing, agro-processing, and energy. Yet unless a young founder clears the high bar of Section 116(5)(c) of Act 896 to get a special Withholding Tax Exemption Certificate, corporate clients still deduct 7.5 per cent from every invoice they issue. Because the startup’s tax rate during the holiday is 0 per cent, every cedi withheld at source becomes a trapped overpayment sitting in the 1.7 per cent refund queue.
If we do not adjust the withholding and provisional tax rules, the same bottleneck will blunt the incentives in the new Startup Bill and the GIPA Act.
Four practical adjustments will bring the tax counter in line with the government's growth agenda:
1. Create a Unified "Pre-Revenue / Dormant Tier" Across ORC and ITAS
Amend Section 126 of the Companies Act (Act 992) and Section 73 of the Revenue Administration Act (Act 915) to give newly incorporated firms a 24-month Pre-Revenue Setup Window. Until a company issues its first commercial invoice or runs payroll above the tax-free threshold, it should file a single, combined annual digital declaration on ORC and ITAS, exempt from external audit fees on zero-revenue accounts and exempt from monthly Nil-return penalties.
2. Issue Automatic Bidding TCCs Upon Filing a Nil Provisional Return
To stop procurement cartels from using shell companies to rig tenders under Act 663, rely on the ORC's Beneficial Ownership register and point-of-payment withholding rather than upfront TCC deposits. Add a clear proviso to Section 14 of Act 915 and Section 122 of Act 896: A newly incorporated entity in its first basis period, or an entity with verified zero chargeable income, shall automatically receive a Digital Bidding Tax Clearance Certificate upon filing a Nil Provisional Return, without requiring an upfront cash deposit. Tax the contract after it is won, not the right to compete for it.
3. Turn Verified Tax Credits into Instant Cross-Tax Offsets on ITAS
While Section 68(1) of Act 915 allows overpayments to offset other tax liabilities, the process is still slowed down by manual approvals and separated from port duties on ICUMS. As GRA scales the ITAS platform, any verified Section 116 withholding credit or overpaid provisional tax should automatically populate a Unified Taxpayer Wallet within 30 days. That allows a growing business to use its tax credits in real time to pay PAYE, VAT, or import duties at Tema Port without waiting on the capped 4 per cent Refund Account.
4. Pair GIPA and Startup Certifications with Automatic Section 116(5)(c) Relief
As Parliament passes the Ghana Startup and Innovation Bill and implements Sections 37 and 38 of the GIPA Act, 2026 (Act 1173), any certified startup on a tax holiday, or any formal MSME with verified net margins below 10 per cent, should automatically receive a digital Section 116(5)(c) Withholding Exemption (or a reduced 1.5 per cent withholding rate) linked directly to its TIN on ITAS.
Ghana has done the hard legislative work of opening the front door to investment through the GIPA Act and the Startup Bill. Now let us clear the tollbooths in the hallway so our young enterprises can actually walk through it.
The author is a Solutionist, Systems Architect, and Technology Associate with IMANI CPE.
